faq.q: Why is hypertension common in Wilms tumour?

exam: A 3‑year‑old presents with a painless left flank mass; what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Obtain an abdominal ultrasound to confirm a solid renal lesion before planning surgery.
How does the presence of aniridia alter your clinical suspicion? — It suggests WAGR syndrome, raising the pre‑test probability of Wilms tumour and prompting genetic counseling.
A child with stage III Wilms tumour is hypertensive; which drug class is preferred and why? — ACE‑inhibitors are first‑line because they block renin‑mediated hypertension and are renal‑protective.
Why is doxorubicin omitted in low‑risk stage I disease? — It adds cardiotoxicity without survival benefit in low‑risk histology.
During surgery the tumour capsule ruptures; what immediate management is required? — Irrigate the peritoneal cavity, give intra‑operative chemotherapy (if protocol allows), and upstage to stage III.

What distinguishes Wilms tumour from neuroblastoma on imaging? — Wilms tumour is confined to the kidney, does not cross the midline, and lacks calcifications; neuroblastoma often crosses midline and shows calcifications.
A patient cannot undergo CT; how do you stage the disease? — Use ultrasound for local staging, chest X‑ray for lung metastases, and rely on surgical pathology for nodal status.
What long‑term complication should you monitor after abdominal radiotherapy? — Secondary malignancies and growth restriction of the irradiated kidney.
ai.title: Wilms Tumour (Nephroblastoma)
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Wilms tumour is the commonest renal malignancy in children, presenting as an abdominal mass with possible haematuria or hypertension. Diagnosis relies on imaging and histology; treatment combines surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy, with staging guiding intensity.

b: Solid, unilateral renal mass in a child
Absence of systemic infection signs
sections.p: Wilms tumour is a malignant embryonal tumour of the kidney arising from nephrogenic rests. Diagnosis requires a solid renal mass on imaging and histological confirmation.

t.b: Is there a renal mass? – Shows a well‑defined, heterogeneous solid lesion; helps differentiate cystic lesions.
What is the tumour size, local invasion and metastasis? – Defines stage, vascular involvement, and lung nodules.
Is the lesion malignant? – Histology confirms Wilms tumour and excludes other small‑round‑blue‑cell tumours.

b: Stage I: confined to kidney, completely resected
Stage II: extends beyond kidney but fully resected
Stage III: residual tumour or nodal disease
Stage IV: distant metastases (lung, liver, bone, brain)
Stage V: bilateral renal disease
sections.p: Staging follows the Children’s Oncology Group (COG) system, based on tumour spill, nodal involvement and distant metastases.

b: WT1 mutation – associated with WAGR (Wilms, Aniridia, Genitourinary malformations, mental Retardation)
WT2 mutation – associated with hemihypertrophy and Beckwith‑Wiedemann syndrome
Denys‑Drash syndrome (WT1) – nephropathy, genital anomalies
sections.p: Most cases are sporadic; 10 % are linked to genetic syndromes that affect renal development.

b: Palpable unilateral flank mass, often discovered by caregiver
Hematuria (microscopic or gross)
Hypertension due to renin secretion
Weight loss or low‑grade fever (late)
sections.p: Children typically present with a painless, enlarging abdominal mass; secondary features arise from tumour pressure or hormone production.
Imaging and laboratory studies guide staging and assess organ function before therapy.

t.b: Are there lung metastases? – Detects pulmonary nodules; if unavailable, consider clinical monitoring.
Is renal function adequate for surgery/chemo? – Guides dosing and need for dialysis.
Is there haematuria? – Supports renal origin; may be absent.
Does the child have a syndrome? – Influences surveillance of contralateral kidney.

b: Sudden increase in abdominal girth with pain – possible tumour rupture
Severe hypertension refractory to medication – risk of encephalopathy
Respiratory distress – large tumour compressing diaphragm
sections.p: Rapid tumour growth or systemic signs demand urgent intervention.

b: Nephrectomy (or partial nephrectomy for bilateral disease) – removes primary tumour.
Vincristine + actinomycin‑D ± doxorubicin – standard chemotherapy; avoid doxorubicin in stage I unless high‑risk histology.
Radiotherapy for stage III/IV or residual disease – reduces local recurrence.
Control hypertension with ACE‑inhibitors; avoid NSAIDs that worsen renal perfusion.
sections.p: Treatment is multimodal: surgery, chemotherapy and, when indicated, radiotherapy.

b: Abdominal ultrasound every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.
Chest imaging (X‑ray or CT) at similar intervals for lung metastasis.
Monitor renal function and blood pressure lifelong, especially after bilateral disease or nephrotoxic chemotherapy.
sections.p: Long‑term surveillance detects recurrence and late effects of therapy.

b: Neuroblastoma – usually adrenal, may cross midline, associated with catecholamine excess.
Rhabdomyosarcoma of the kidney – rarer, more infiltrative, often with skeletal muscle markers.
Renal cystic disease – multilocular cysts, non‑solid on imaging.
sections.p: Other paediatric abdominal masses can mimic Wilms tumour.

b: Normal urine dipstick does not exclude microscopic haematuria; repeat microscopy if suspicion remains.
Chest X‑ray may miss tiny pulmonary metastases; CT is more sensitive if available.
sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden abdominal pain with distension – possible tumour rupture
Respiratory compromise from large intra‑abdominal mass
